---
title: "020 — RC UI verification"
---

> **Status:** standing

**Goal.** Replace the manual quiz-and-labs pass on every release candidate with
automated, deterministic verification: a browser deck driving the real app
through onboarding → chat → quiz generation → every question type → both
grading outcomes → lab completion, plus a logic-layer suite for depth a browser
cannot affordably reach. The work began as idea 007-rc-ui-verification, whose
decisions.md verdict chose a user-defined hybrid — the Playwright deck as
spine, the logic-not-browser card as complement — and folded in two owner
refinements: a read-only generation-prompt contract, and the mock's
deterministic grading lever.

**Why.** Manual RC passes are repeat-on-every-tag chores — slow, inconsistently
applied, and growing with the features. The stand-in from [017 — mock-LLM chat
tests](017-mock-llm-chat-tests.qmd) answered every request with the same chat
reply, which blocked all quiz/labs verification on day one; teaching it
request-kind discrimination was the bulk of the work, not an edge case. The
feature's one deliberate product change was user-ruled against 017's
zero-diff spirit: the format/contract sections of the quiz and lab generation
prompts — which the parser's output contract depends on — were user-editable
settings values, a silent-breakage risk for real users and for the mock's
classification alike.

**Outcome & reversals.** Merged as PR #33 (2026-09-06). The mock classifies
requests exclusively on code-owned, user-un-influenceable bytes — the stream
flag, the `json` tool's description, `startsWith` against code-owned contract
openings — and serves a deterministic fixture per kind; unknown kinds get a
loud 400 with diagnostic hints, never a wrong-fixture reply that would
manufacture a false green. The grading lever keys on submitted answer text
("should be correct" / "should be wrong", conservative `false` default) and is
asserted end to end through the real UI, proving trigger phrases survive the
app's answer handling. The contract became a code constant with custom
instructions appended after it and legacy whole-prompt overrides migrated on
read — read-only by construction, not by UI enforcement. Two quiet
determinism traps were designed around rather than patched: MCQ options
legitimately shuffle per run, so the deck asserts payload-driven (by answer
text, never position) instead of seeding the RNG, which would have been a
test-only product mode; and classification anchors on contract openings
because prepended context notes defeat substring matching. The logic suite
covers parse→persist, every grading bucket (true/false/null via `GradeError`),
and failure paths — corrective retries ending in typed generation errors.
The wire classification and prompt-assembly rules are preserved verbatim at
[appendices/020-mock-llm-protocol.md](appendices/020-mock-llm-protocol.md) and
[appendices/020-prompt-settings-contract.md](appendices/020-prompt-settings-contract.md),
pinned to the product constants by a marker test.

**Learnings.**

- Classify requests only on bytes users cannot influence — code-owned contract
  sections make discrimination as trustworthy as the constants themselves.
- Unknown must fail loudly: a mock that falls back to the wrong fixture
  produces exactly the false greens verification exists to prevent.
- Read-only-by-construction (a code constant) is the only contract protection
  that holds against every write path; UI-level enforcement is cosmetic.
- Assert payloads, not positions, when the product legitimately randomizes —
  test-mode seeding would smuggle a test-only mode into the product.
- The browser deck and the logic suite are complements: only the browser
  witnesses the proxy hop and key path, only the logic layer reaches every
  grading bucket and failure path affordably.
